name: Laggori
confidence_why: Alamin Mubarak (2006) describes Laggori as a stress language with no tone but leaves stress uninvestigated and gives no placement rule, whereas Tucker & Bryan (1966) report three tone levels for the Daju group, Manfredi (2013, 2022) transcribes Laggori with high and falling tones, and Dimmendaal (2015) calls for phonetic investigation before the stress analysis is accepted, so even the type of prosodic system is contested and no source says where stress falls.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Alamin (2006) says Laggori has no tone and is a stress language, but gives no placement rule and says stress needs further investigation. This conflicts with Tucker & Bryan 1966 (Daju group incl. Liguri: three tone levels; stress of some importance, not investigated) and with Manfredi 2013 as summarised by Wikipedia (tonal, high and falling tones; Manfredi's own 2022 Laggori data are tone-marked). Dimmendaal 2015 explicitly doubts the stress analysis. No source states where stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Alamin flags stress as uninvestigated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; the sources are noun-morphology and loanword studies, not prosodic descriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern sources describe 'Laggori/Laggorí' (= Liguri proper, lÓgørik), one of the three closely related dialects of the Liguri cluster (Liguri, Saburi, Tallau; Stevenson 1964:111 via Boyeldieu); Alamin 2006 and Manfredi 2013/2015 worked with Laggorí speakers displaced to Khartoum. Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat Shatt and Liguri jointly as 'Eastern Daju' with Shatt-based data. Glottolog logo1261 covers the whole cluster; no separate glottocodes for Saburi/Tallau.

new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's DAJU chapter covers the whole Daju group (Eastern: SHATT and LIGURI; Western: DAJU [Darfur, Sila] and NJALGULGULE) and states that Stevenson's material 'deals mainly with SHATT, from which the majority of examples are consequently taken'; the Tone and Stress statement is thus a group-level remark grounded in Shatt (shat1244), not a description of Liguri/Logorik (logo1261) specifically. Liguri = Laggori = Logorik (ISO liu) per our earlier reading notes.

new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's Daju chapter describes the Daju group as a whole; its examples are 'mainly SHATT' (Shatt = Caning, shat1244) per p. 231, with LIGURI (= Logorik/Laggori, logo1261, Nuba Mountains) named only as the second Eastern Daju member; the tone-and-stress sentence is therefore group-level and at best indirect evidence for Laggori. Alamin Mubarak 2006 describes Laggori proper (speakers of the Sudan Local Language Club, Khartoum).

readall_conflicts: Tucker & Bryan 1966 (Daju group, Shatt-based, p. 232) report three tone levels but no tonal doublets, plus stress of 'some importance' left uninvestigated; Alamin Mubarak 2006 (Laggori, pp. 12-13, snippet already held by the project) says there is no tone and Laggori is a stress language, with stress needing further investigation; Manfredi 2013 as summarised by Wikipedia describes Laggori as tonal (high and falling tones), and Dimmendaal 2015 flags Alamin's stress analysis as needing phonetic investigation. The sources therefore disagree on whether the language is tonal or stress-based, and no source gives a stress-placement rule. No new disagreement. The one work in this bundle (Tucker & Bryan 1966, ch. Daju, p. 232) could be read only at snippet level, and its text is the statement already held by the project: three tone levels noted (no tonal doublets), stress 'would also seem to have some importance, but has not been fully investigated', stated for the Daju group with data mainly from Shatt, no placement given. That stands against Alamin Mubarak 2006 (pp. 12-13: 'There is no tone in Laggori. It is a stress language. The issue of stress needs further investigation.') on the question of tone, which is the conflict the catalog already records (classification conflict)
